objection: If Jesus is God, why did he pray to God?
answer:
Friend, thank you for pressing this honestly — it deserves a careful answer, not a dismissal. You're right that prayer implies distinction of persons: the Son addresses the Father, asks something of Him, and is sent by Him. That is exactly what orthodox faith affirms — not two gods, one greater and one lesser, but one God in three distinct persons, of whom the Son is truly man as well as truly God. In Gethsemane, it is the incarnate Son, in His human nature and human will, crying out to the Father; the same Person who could say "before Abraham was, I am" now also says "not my will, but thine be done," because He has taken up a real human nature that shrinks from suffering and death. This is not evidence against His deity but the very meaning of incarnation — true God has become true man, and prays as a man while remaining, in His person, the eternal Son.

John 17:3 does distinguish the Father and the Son personally — it must, since they are distinct persons — but distinction is not exclusion from deity. The same Gospel that records this prayer opens by declaring the Word was God and closes with Thomas kneeling before the risen Christ confessing "My Lord and my God." Jesus is sent, yes — but being sent describes the order of persons within the Godhead, the Father as origin and the Son as the one who comes forth, not a difference of rank in nature. Notably, the earliest Jewish Christians, heirs of the Shema, who would rather die than give worship to a creature, nonetheless prayed directly to Jesus — Stephen dying with "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit," the Church crying "Maranatha, our Lord, come." That they prayed *to* Him even while He prayed *to the Father* shows they saw no contradiction: the Son who prays as man is also the Lord who is prayed to as God.

# The Prayer Objection

Brother, this troubles me deeply. If Jesus is truly God, how can he pray? In Gethsemane he cries out, "My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me" — begging his Father to change what will happen. A servant prays to his master; a son prays to his father. But God prays to no one. God submits to no will but his own. When Jesus says in John 17:3, "This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" — he separates himself from God, calls God *the* God, and speaks of himself as *sent*. How is the sent one equal to the one who sends? Does God send God? This is not the language of equality; it is the language of a prophet speaking to his Lord.

Friend, thank you for pressing this honestly — it deserves a careful answer, not a dismissal. You're right that prayer implies distinction of persons: the Son addresses the Father, asks something of Him, and is sent by Him. That is exactly what orthodox faith affirms — not two gods, one greater and one lesser, but one God in three distinct persons, of whom the Son is truly man as well as truly God.
